content: Arum maculatum, a plant belonging to the family Araceae, is commonly found in the temperate regions of northern Europe. It is also referred to as lords-and-ladies or cuckoo pint. This plant typically grows in shaded hedgerows and woodlands. During the spring months of April and May, its leaves, often marked with purple spots, emerge, followed by its flowers. These flowers are borne on a poker-shaped inflorescence known as a spadix, which is partially enclosed by a pale green, leaf-like structure called a spathe. The flowers themselves are not visible externally, as they are clustered at the base of the spadix. Female flowers form a ring at the bottom, while male flowers are situated above them. Above the male flowers, there is a ring of hair-like structures that act as an insect trap. Insects become trapped beneath this ring of hairs, where they are dusted with pollen from the male flowers. Once they escape, they carry the pollen to the spadices of other plants, facilitating the pollination of the female flowers. While the spadix is most commonly purple, it can also appear yellow in some cases. In the autumn, the female flowers develop into a cluster of bright red berries, which persist even after the spathe and other leaves have withered. These berries are highly toxic. The plant's root tuber, which can grow to a significant size and may be located as deep as 400 mm below the ground, serves as a storage organ for starch. All parts of Arum maculatum can provoke allergic reactions in many individuals, necessitating careful handling. Interestingly, small rodents are often attracted to the spadix, and it is not uncommon to find plants with portions of the spadix eaten away. The spadix generates heat and likely emits a scent as the flowers mature, which may explain its appeal to rodents. In the British Isles, Arum maculatum is also known as cuckoo pint, a name that dates back to Nicholas Culpeper's 16th-century herbal. This name is shared with another native British Arum species, Arum italicum, also called Italian lords-and-ladies. Historically, the roasted root of the cuckoo pint was considered edible and was once traded under the name Portland sago. It was used similarly to salop or salep, a popular working-class beverage before the widespread adoption of tea and coffee. Additionally, it served as a substitute for arrowroot.
